bear_thesis_sentence: Cerebras is a single-customer hardware company wearing an inference-cloud costume, priced at 102x sales with a tiny float that masks a lock-up flood, and the stock halves when growth decelerates into a post-IPO unlock.
thesis_under_attack: Bulls believe Cerebras is the wafer-scale winner of the inference era, that its speed lead compounds into a multi-billion recurring cloud business, and that customer concentration fades as enterprise logos pile in fast enough to justify a 102x sales multiple.

bear_breakers.title: G42 is the business, and it sits in a geopolitical crossfire
bear_breakers.body: The 2024 S-1 showed G42, a single UAE customer, at roughly 83-87% of revenue. A company where one Gulf buyer is five-sixths of the top line is not a diversified franchise; it is a vendor-financed bet on one relationship. G42 has its own ties to both US and Chinese spheres, and US export-control scrutiny of advanced compute sold into the Gulf is rising. If Washington restricts the flow, or if G42 builds or buys elsewhere, revenue does not dip, it collapses. You see it coming in the 10-K concentration footnote and any 8-K on export licensing.

bear_breakers.title: 102x trailing sales has to be fed by impossible numbers
bear_breakers.body: At ~$52B market cap on $510M revenue, the stock trades at 102x sales. To grow into even 15x sales in three years, revenue must roughly hit $3.5B, a 7x in 36 months off a base that just decelerated from 269% growth (2024) to 76% (2025). Multiple compression alone, from 102x to a still-rich 30x, is a 70% drawdown if revenue merely doubles. The math doesn't agree with the price unless hypergrowth not only continues but reaccelerates.

bear_breakers.title: Lock-up unlock against an 8.67M-share float
bear_breakers.body: Float is roughly 8.67M shares against ~219.6M shares implied outstanding. That means about 96% of the equity is locked. A thin float manufactures the high price; when the IPO lock-up expires, insiders, pre-IPO funds and employees can sell into a market that was never tested for real supply. Post-IPO unlocks on hot AI names have repeatedly cut prices 30-50% within weeks. The unlock date is the single most predictable catalyst, and it points down.

bear_breakers.title: The 2025 'profit' is an accounting mirage
bear_breakers.body: Net income was +$237.8M in 2025 while operating income was -$145.3M. The gap is non-operating: warrant or preferred remeasurement, tax items, one-offs. The real engine still loses money at the operating line on $510M of revenue. Anyone underwriting 'Cerebras is profitable' off the net income line is reading a number that reverses. Operating margin was -29% in 2025.

bear_breakers.title: Growth is already decelerating fast
bear_breakers.body: Revenue grew 220% (2023), 269% (2024), then 76% (2025). The second derivative turned hard. Each step down in growth rate compresses a 102x multiple violently. The Condor Galaxy buildout is largely a one-time installation cycle; once G42's clusters are delivered, the comparable gets brutal and the hardware line can go flat or negative year-on-year.

bear_breakers.title: Single architecture, deep-pocketed competition
bear_breakers.body: Cerebras bets everything on wafer-scale. Nvidia's Blackwell and Rubin roadmaps, plus inference specialists Groq and SambaNova, plus hyperscaler in-house silicon (Trainium, TPU, MTIA, Maia) all target the same inference dollars. Cerebras spent $243M on R&D in 2025; Nvidia spends that in days. A speed benchmark lead is not a moat when the competition has 100x the R&D budget and owns the developer ecosystem (CUDA). One architecture means one point of failure.

bear_breakers.title: Inference is becoming a price war, not a margin pool
bear_breakers.body: Per-token inference pricing has been falling steeply as Groq, Together, Fireworks, and the hyperscalers compete and as open models commoditize serving. Cerebras's 39% gross margin is thin for a 'software-like' story, and a token price war pressures the exact line the bull case needs to expand. Speed leadership doesn't guarantee pricing power when buyers can route to good-enough endpoints at half the cost.

bear_breakers.title: Negative book equity and a cash burn that the IPO only delays
bear_breakers.body: Stockholders equity was -$579M at year-end 2025 and free cash flow was deeply negative (operating cash flow near breakeven only after working-capital swings tied to G42 prepayments). The IPO refilled the tank, but a company still losing money operationally while ramping WSE-4 will burn it. If capital markets cool, the next raise is dilutive at a far lower price.

bear_breakers.title: Customer prepayments flatter the cash flow
bear_breakers.body: G42-style upfront commitments inflate deferred revenue and operating cash flow in the ramp years, which makes the cash statement look better than the underlying unit economics. When the prepayment cycle laps, cash conversion deteriorates even if revenue holds. This is a classic place where concentrated-customer hardware names look healthier than they are right before a reset.

bear_breakers.title: Sell-side has no anchor and the stock is round-trip prone
bear_breakers.body: yfinance returns no consensus target and no analyst count, so price discovery is being set by a thin float and momentum, not fundamental coverage. The stock already ran from $196 to $386 and back to $238 inside a year. That volatility profile, 49% peak-to-trough, is a momentum vehicle, and momentum vehicles unwind when the growth narrative stalls.

bear_paragraph: Strip the wafer-scale romance and Cerebras is a hardware company where one UAE customer was roughly five-sixths of revenue, priced at 102 times sales, with 96% of its shares still locked. Each of those facts is dangerous on its own; together they're a setup. Growth already decelerated from 269% to 76%, and the Condor Galaxy installations that drove the ramp are a finite buildout, not an annuity. The 2025 net income headline is an accounting artifact: operating margin was -29%, and the company still loses money making and selling its product. The catalysts that matter point down. The IPO lock-up expires against an 8.67M-share float, and post-IPO unlocks on hot AI names routinely cut prices 30-50% within weeks of real supply hitting the tape. Export-control scrutiny of advanced compute sold into the Gulf is tightening, and a single 8-K on G42 licensing could erase the revenue base. Meanwhile Nvidia, Groq, SambaNova and every hyperscaler's in-house chip are crowding the same inference dollars while per-token prices fall. A 70% drawdown needs nothing exotic: multiple compression from 102x toward a still-generous 30x, plus one growth disappointment or one unlock. The bear case doesn't require a recession. It requires the float to normalize and the law of large numbers to do its work.
structural_concerns: Customer concentration: G42 was roughly 83-87% of revenue per the 2024 S-1; one Gulf buyer dominates the top line and carries US export-control exposure.
Float distortion: ~8.67M shares float versus ~219.6M shares outstanding (about 96% locked), so the quoted price has not been tested against real supply ahead of the IPO lock-up expiry.
Profitability gap: operating income -$145.3M (margin -29%) in 2025 versus a +$237.8M net income headline driven by non-operating items; the operating business still loses money.

key_risks.title: Single-customer dependence
key_risks.description: G42 at roughly 83-87% of 2023 revenue per the S-1. Any pause, renegotiation, or substitution by this one UAE buyer takes the majority of revenue with it. Diversification is claimed but unverified in the available data, and even a diversified mix would still be small in absolute terms.

key_risks.title: Lock-up overhang on a thin float
key_risks.description: About 96% of shares are locked against an 8.67M-share float. The high quoted price is partly a scarcity artifact. The IPO lock-up expiry is a predictable, dateable supply shock that has crushed comparable AI IPOs within weeks.

key_risks.title: Export controls on Gulf compute
key_risks.description: US scrutiny of advanced AI compute sold into the UAE and broader Gulf is rising. Cerebras's largest revenue stream flows to a UAE customer. A licensing restriction or denial would directly cut the revenue base, and the risk is binary and outside management's control.

key_risks.title: Growth deceleration into a tough comp
key_risks.description: Revenue growth fell from 269% (2024) to 76% (2025). The Condor Galaxy buildout is a finite installation cycle. As it laps, the hardware line can stall, and a 102x sales multiple offers no cushion for a deceleration the numbers already show.

key_risks.title: Single-architecture bet versus better-funded rivals
key_risks.description: Everything rides on wafer-scale. Nvidia (CUDA plus Blackwell/Rubin), Groq, SambaNova and hyperscaler in-house silicon all chase the same inference dollars with vastly larger R&D. Cerebras's $243M R&D budget is a rounding error against Nvidia's. One architecture is one point of failure.

key_risks.title: Cash burn and financing risk
key_risks.description: Negative book equity (-$579M) and operating losses mean the IPO cash gets consumed during the WSE-4 ramp. If equity markets cool, the next raise is dilutive at a lower price, and customer prepayments that flatter today's cash flow reverse as the cycle laps.

what_shorts_are_saying: No published activist short reports (Hindenburg, Muddy Waters, etc.) were found via available skills as of 2026-06-09. The bearish commentary that exists centers on three points: the G42 customer concentration disclosed in the S-1, the 102x trailing sales valuation, and the lock-up/float dynamics typical of a hot AI IPO. Sell-side coverage is thin enough that yfinance returns no mean target, which itself signals a price set by flow rather than fundamentals.
historical_precedent: Concentrated-customer hardware IPOs at extreme multiples have a poor record. Arm and Astera Labs ran hard post-IPO then gave back large chunks on lock-up and growth normalization. More pointed: Cerebras rhymes with the 2021 SPAC AI-hardware cohort and with names like Nikola and Lordstown where a single anchor relationship and a thin float propped a valuation that reverted once supply normalized. The closest functional precedent is any AI IPO where 90%+ of shares were locked: the post-unlock supply shock is the consistent killer, and Cerebras checks that box with a 8.67M-share float.

bear_dcf_assumptions.wacc_reasoning: Bear-side cost of capital reflects customer concentration, single-architecture risk, export exposure and a high beta. 12.5% is 200bps above a typical bull-case semi number.
bear_dcf_assumptions.terminal_growth_reasoning: Below-GDP terminal if the G42 relationship breaks or competition commoditizes inference; the long-run franchise is not assured.
bear_dcf_assumptions.fcf_growth_path: revenue +40 / +20 / +10 / +6 / +4, FCF margin reaching only mid-teens as a token price war caps gross margin
bear_dcf_assumptions.fcf_growth_reasoning: Deceleration accelerates as the Condor Galaxy cycle laps and competition compresses pricing; FCF turns positive late and stays thin rather than ramping to a software-like margin.

what_would_change_my_mind: A 10-K showing G42 down to under 40% of revenue with named enterprise logos each contributing real dollars, gross margin moving through the mid-40s on cloud mix, and an operating line approaching breakeven, all before the lock-up unlock clears.
